h1: Brewing your first beer with a friend: kit, costs and jobs split
title: Brewing Your First Beer With a Friend | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew your first beer with a friend: what kit to share, how to split costs fairly, who does which job on brew day and how to share the beer.
teaser: Two people, one pot, half the cost. Brewing with a friend is the easiest way to start, if you agree on a few things first.
standfirst: Homebrewing is more fun with company. Splitting the starter kit makes the first step cheaper. It also needs a little planning. Who keeps the kit? Who pays for what? Who cleans? Settle those early and you will both enjoy brewing far more.
sections: Why brewing with a friend works

A brew day has quiet moments and busy ones. During the mash and the boil, there is plenty of time to talk. At the start of the boil, when the wort foams, or at the end, when everything needs cooling, sanitising and moving at once, two pairs of hands make a real difference.

Brewing with someone also helps you learn. One of you reads the recipe while the other measures. You notice each other's mistakes. You argue about whether the beer tastes fruity or solventy, which is exactly how tasters build a shared vocabulary.
The kit you actually need to share

For a first brew in a bag batch of about 10 litres, the essentials are:

  • A 15 to 20 litre stainless steel stockpot
  • A grain bag that fits the pot
  • A digital thermometer and a hydrometer with its test jar
  • A food grade fermenter with a lid and an airlock
  • A siphon, tubing and a bottling wand
  • No rinse sanitiser and a brewery cleaner
  • Bottles, caps and a capper

Many people already own a large pot. Ask before you buy. Our guide to a homebrewing starter kit in India lists what to look for and where to economise. The brew in a bag method needs the least equipment of any all grain approach.

There are two kinds of spending: equipment you buy once and ingredients you buy every batch.

  • Equipment: split it evenly and agree who keeps it at their home. The person who stores it carries the hassle, so the other might cover a larger share of the first ingredients.
  • Ingredients: split each batch evenly. Split the beer evenly too.
  • Write it down. A shared note or spreadsheet of who paid for what saves arguments later. It also tells you what a batch really costs.

Agree now what happens if one of you loses interest or moves city. The simplest rule is that the person who leaves sells their share of the kit to the other at an agreed price, or you sell it and split the money.

Pick something forgiving for batch one. A pale ale or an amber ale with a clean dry yeast is a good choice. Both ferment happily at temperatures you can manage at home and show you clearly whether the process worked. Leave the hazy IPA, the lager and the mango beer for later, when you both trust your sanitising and your temperature control.

Agree on the recipe before you buy anything. Then buy exactly what it lists. Two beginners who each add one favourite ingredient end up with a beer neither of them can learn from. Keep the first batch simple, take notes and argue about the second one.
Splitting the jobs on brew day

Give each person a clear role so nothing is missed:

  • Brewer: heats the water, mashes, watches temperatures and runs the boil and hop additions.
  • Cellar hand: cleans and sanitises the fermenter, chiller and anything that touches cooled wort, takes the hydrometer readings and keeps the brew log.

Swap roles on the next batch so you both learn everything. Sanitising is the job most likely to be rushed. It is also the one that most affects the beer. Make it someone's clear responsibility.

The fermenter lives in one home for two weeks. The person keeping it is responsible for temperature. In warm weather that means a water bath and frozen bottles, checked morning and evening. A simple message with the temperature each day keeps the other person involved.

Bottle together. It is the most hands on job and goes twice as fast with one person filling and one capping. Split the bottles evenly. Keep two from each batch to taste side by side a month later. Comparing notes on what worked is where you both get better.

Most first brews go wrong in the same few ways: fermenting too warm, cutting corners on sanitising and bottling too early. Our guide to first homebrew mistakes covers them in detail. Two people catch more of these than one, as long as each knows what to watch for.
faqs: How much kit do two people need to start brewing?
One set is enough for two. A stockpot, grain bag, thermometer, hydrometer, fermenter, siphon, sanitiser and bottling gear will do.
Who should keep the shared brewing kit?
Whoever has the space and a cooler spot for fermenting. The other person can cover a larger share of ingredients to balance it out.
How should we split the beer?
Evenly, with a couple of bottles set aside from each batch to taste together later.
Is it better to brew alone or with a friend?
Brewing with a friend is cheaper, easier on brew day and you learn faster from each other's questions and mistakes.
